title: Booking for Shaw: what Calloway taught him
summary: He explains why booking appealed, how Cab's work taught him to book, and that Bill Davis wouldn't listen when getting twenty-five hundred dollars.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Managers, bookers and the business of getting work

blocks.x: And you know, all the time I was looking at teaching. That's why I studied with Timothy. His office was next door to me. I used to go in and get my books and practice in his office. And man, I'm so grateful to that man.
So what else happened with your booking now? Who else did you...?
So I got over there at Shaw, and I started booking. I knew how to book already, but here I had an office with a lot of big attractions. And I had the Eastern District, which...
How much money could you make with that, Foots? More than you can make playing, right?
Well, not necessarily. But it was something I wanted to learn. I wanted to learn the booking business for some reason, because I...
Even at the sacrifice of giving up playing?

Well, it was hard to do both. I did a little teaching. Every now and then, I'd have some guy come in town and I'd go over to the studio and give him a lesson and come back. I'd do it on my lunch hour. But it was just a challenge I got involved with. I made a lot of money with it because I could hustle...

And there's one thing... I got so mad at all the extra work I had to do with Calloway. But man, when I got out of that band and got on my own, all that knowledge paid off. It just paid off like clockwork. Because I didn't realize it until I got involved and started making that money, you know. And the knowledge I learned about how a band need to dress... The first thing you needed to do is perform. And see, I knew my music; when someone played good, I knew he was good -- and it's just a matter of directing his career. If Bill would have listened to me more, I could have made him a big star. Because he had three pieces, and I was getting twenty-five hundred dollars for him. And he had
Twenty-five hundred dollars, when he just started out, getting them records. And he was a hard listener. He wouldn't listen to me.

That was in the Fifties, in the late Fifties. See, he had these good musicians, and to keep them good musicians, all he had to do when he started making more was give them a little bit of a taste. Because the other guys contributed as much as he did. Because Bill Jennings was a genius.
